name: Jesuit Refugee Service: programmes (charityevals' estimate)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: JRS's 2025 programme expenses by region (Annual Report 2025, p. 33: West Africa $18.4m, Eastern Africa $14.8m, Middle East $8.5m, Latin America $6.7m, Asia Pacific $5.7m, South Asia $1.6m, Europe $23.3m, North America $4.1m), each region spread over its main country programmes by a judgment (Chad, the DRC, Kenya, South Sudan, Lebanon and Italy largest); the branches' results aren't split by country, so this weights every country by its spending.
summary: The Jesuit Refugee Service (JRS) spent $93.6 million in 2025 serving 1.09 million refugees and other displaced people in 57 countries: schools in refugee camps and host communities (43% of programme spending), livelihoods, emergency aid, legal advice and protection, mental health and psychosocial support, pastoral care, reconciliation and a little health care; its advocacy is a separate model. JRS counts the people each programme served but publishes no controlled evaluation or outcome data, so every programme is built from its spending, its reach and the research on its kind of work, and counted at half by the shared missing-data slider. It comes to about {{result}} years of healthy life per $1,000 (plausible range {{range}}), because education carries over 90% of the result: JRS runs whole school years for camp children who would otherwise have none, where NRC's education is mostly short activities. The result is mostly uncertainty, chiefly how much of JRS's education is schooling children would otherwise lack and how much learning raises later earnings; the spending is the network-wide summary in its annual report, not audited accounts.

sections.title: Effect per unit

sections.title: Adjustments
sections.explainer: Discounts for weaker evidence, what would have happened anyway, credit shared with others, and delivery falling short. All multiply the outcome.

sections.title: Other outcomes, in this model's unit
sections.explainer: charityevals' standard step for outcomes in more than one unit (docs/normalization.md 2.6): each outcome is counted in its own unit (units of value for income and deaths, WELLBYs for life satisfaction, tonnes of CO₂e, chicken pain days) and put into this model's unit by its unit's conversion over this unit's, which the headline's conversion cancels. So each moves only with its own sliders, exactly as in a model of its own unit. The rows are fixed; don't edit them.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.explainer: The outcome in the family's shared unit, per dollar.

sections.title: Your dollar's share
sections.explainer: Staff who earn less than they could elsewhere pay part of the cost in kind. With credit by share of resources, your dollar is credited with its share of the full cost only.

rows.label: Emergency aid: cost per person served, including overhead
rows.explainer: About $115. Context: education about $80 a participant, livelihoods about $260 (JRS's own 2024 figure, $203 a person a year before overhead, p. 17).

rows.label: Emergency aid: death rate among the people served in low-income crises, without the response
rows.explainer: Judgment 0.02 (0.012-0.04) a person-year: Sphere's emergency threshold is a crude death rate of 1 per 10,000 a day (0.037 a year); JRS's emergency aid in 2025 ran from acute displacement (Sudanese arrivals in Renk and eastern Chad, eastern DRC) to protracted camps close to the baseline.

rows.label: Emergency aid: death rate in the same populations before the crisis
rows.explainer: The crude death rates of the countries behind JRS's largest African emergency work (Sudanese refugees in Chad and South Sudan, the DRC; UN World Population Prospects via the site's country facts), so only excess deaths count.

rows.label: Emergency aid: share of the excess deaths the response averts among the people served
rows.explainer: Judgment 2% (0.5-6%): food, household items, cash and shelter raise consumption, and some excess deaths are from hunger, exposure and their diseases, but JRS runs no nutrition treatment and little health care, which avert most of a response's deaths. As charityevals' NRC food security (2%); reference class 0.75% for MSF's item distributions, 2% for ShelterBox's shelter, 4% for Save the Children's response with health and nutrition.

rows.label: Emergency aid: years of the crisis the help covers per person
rows.explainer: Judgment half a year (3-12 months): distributions, cash and transit accommodation usually cover the first months after displacement or a lean season.

rows.label: Emergency aid: deaths averted per person served in a low-income crisis (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: Excess deaths over the months covered, times the share the help averts.

rows.label: Emergency aid: share of the people served in low- and middle-income crises
rows.explainer: Judgment 65% (50-80%), anchored on JRS's spending: its southern regions (Africa, the Middle East, Latin America, Asia) spent $55.7m of $83.9m in 2025 (66%, p. 33), Europe and North America $27.4m. The rest of the emergency help is accommodation and urgent support for asylum seekers and evacuees in Europe and North America, where no crisis mortality is averted.

rows.label: Emergency aid: deaths averted per person served, all regions (before adjustments)
Share of the deaths averted that are of children under five
rows.explainer: The excess deaths emergency aid averts in displacement crises are mostly from malnutrition and the infections it worsens, diarrhoea foremost; the site's age split of diarrhoeal deaths in sub-Saharan Africa (WHO Global Health Estimates, facts/death_ages.json) stands in for them: 55% under five, within the 40-60% that crisis mortality surveys give (the under-five death rate about twice the crude rate). The site has no all-cause crisis split; the age shares move the result by under 1%.

rows.label: Of the deaths averted at five or older, share aged 5 to 14
rows.explainer: The rest of the same split, band by band: 5-14 as a share of deaths at five or older.

rows.label: Of the deaths averted at 15 or older, share aged 15 to 49
rows.explainer: The rest of the same split; deaths at 50 and over valued at GiveWell's 50-74 weight.

rows.label: Value of a crisis death averted (units of value)
rows.explainer: The site's one value of a death, by age band, times your value of a life.

rows.label: Emergency aid: illness averted per person served in a low-income crisis, in DALYs (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: Judgment 0.0005 DALYs (0-0.002): malnutrition, exposure and their infections averted among those who don't die, beyond the consumption valued below; small because the help is a few months of goods or cash, not treatment. As NRC's food security.

rows.label: Emergency aid: illness averted per person served, all regions, in DALYs
Emergency aid: share of the line's spending that reaches people as cash, goods or accommodation
rows.explainer: Judgment 50% (35-70%): JRS publishes no split of costs by type; NRC's costs were 61% materials and transfers across all its lines, and JRS's work leans more on staff (accompaniment, case work), but emergency aid is its most goods-heavy line. The rest pays the staff who deliver it.

rows.label: Emergency aid: cash, goods and accommodation delivered per person in the year (US$)
rows.explainer: The line's spending that reaches people, per person served: about {{row:value_delivered_per_person}}. Counted in full as consumption: deaths averted are a small share of the value (2% of excess deaths), so the overlap is negligible.

rows.label: US prices in 2017 relative to 2025
rows.explainer: Puts 2025 dollars into 2017 prices, the year of the PPP factors and the baseline.

rows.label: US prices in 2024 relative to 2025
rows.explainer: Puts 2025 dollars into 2024 prices, the year of the UK consumption figure.

rows.label: PPP conversion (2017 international $ per US $), JRS's African crises
rows.explainer: The same three countries as the baseline death rate (World Bank, via the site's country facts). Sudan's stands in for eastern Chad, where many of the Sudanese refugees JRS serves live: the site has no PPP factor for Chad; the choice moves the result by under 1%.

rows.label: Emergency aid: consumption per person per year of the people served in low-income crises (2017 PPP $)
rows.explainer: Judgment $700 PPP a year ($400-1,200): displaced households in low-income countries, around the extreme-poverty line ($2.15 a day, $785 a year).

rows.label: Emergency aid: ln(consumption) gain per person served in a low-income crisis
rows.formula: years_exposed * ln(1 + value_delivered_per_person * cpi_2017_vs_2025 * ppp_factor / (baseline_consumption * years_exposed))
rows.explainer: The goods on the site's one log-income scale over the months they are used: years_exposed × ln(1 + value ÷ the consumption of those months).

rows.label: Emergency aid: asylum seekers' consumption as a share of the average in Europe
rows.explainer: Judgment 15% (8-30%): asylum seekers JRS houses and supports in Europe live on reception allowances well below the national average; the UK's asylum support is £49.18 a person a week (gov.uk, Asylum support: what you'll get, https://www.gov.uk/asylum-support/what-youll-get), about $3,300 a year against about $27,000 average survey consumption, 12%, plus housing in kind. The UK stands in for JRS's European and North American countries (the site has no consumption figure for most of them).

rows.label: Emergency aid: consumption per person per year of asylum seekers served in Europe and North America (2024 US$)
rows.explainer: The UK's household consumption per person from the national accounts, put on the household-survey scale by the site's shared ratio, times the recipients' share.

rows.label: Emergency aid: ln(consumption) gain per person served in Europe and North America
Emergency aid: ln(consumption) gain per person served, all regions
Education: learning gain of programmes improving schooling children already get (SD)

source.title: Evans & Yuan (2022), How Big Are Effect Sizes in International Education Studies?, Educational Evaluation and Policy Analysis, doi:10.3102/01623737221079646
source.quote: We identify a median effect size of 0.10 standard deviations on learning and 0.07 standard deviations on access among randomized controlled trials.

rows.explainer: The median effect on learning of randomised evaluations of education programmes in low- and middle-income countries (Evans and Yuan 2022), 0.10 SD, mostly programmes improving schooling children already attend; the range from light activities (language classes, early childhood play) at 0.03 to well-run teacher training and remedial programmes at 0.2. Used for the participants not in schooling they would otherwise lack (edu_access_share). JRS publishes no controlled evaluation of its own education.

rows.label: Education: share of participants in schooling they would otherwise lack
rows.explainer: Judgment 25% (10-45%): JRS runs formal schools in refugee camps and settlements, where most children have no other school (it is UNHCR's lead education partner in 19 camps in eastern Chad, Annual Report 2024 printed p. 14 (PDF p. 8), 'delivering a wide range of services in 19 refugee camps'; schools in Kakuma, South Sudan and Lebanon, 2025 report pp. 12-15), and accelerated learning for children who missed years; it also counts teacher training, language and vocational classes and early childhood activities. It publishes no count of pupils in its formal schools, so there is no number to anchor on: the share is a judgment, wide. The 2024 statement about Chad predates the 2025 US cuts, which ended US funding for JRS Chad's camp secondary schools, so the best guess is below a third.

rows.label: Education: learning gain from a year of schooling for children otherwise out of school (SD)
rows.explainer: Judgment 0.5 SD (0.25-0.65): the randomised trial of village-based schools in Afghanistan (Burde and Linden 2013, American Economic Journal: Applied Economics 5(3), https://doi.org/10.1257/app.5.3.27) found girls' test scores 0.65 and boys' 0.40 standard deviations higher when schooling replaced none; 0.5 for a mix of girls and boys; displaced children move and drop out more, so the low end is half that.

rows.label: Education: average learning gain per participant (SD)
Education: adult earnings gain per SD of skill still there in adult life
rows.explainer: The site's one figure for low- and middle-income countries (@education.earnings_gain_per_sd_adult_skills_lmic: 20%, 10% to 30%), from the Center for Global Development's review of the studies linking adults' reading and maths to their earnings, per SD of skill still there in adult life.

rows.label: Education: share of the learning gain still there in adult life
rows.explainer: The site's one figure (@education.test_gain_persistence_to_adulthood: {{row:edu_persistence}}, 20% to 70%): test-score gains fade, a fifth to a half of a year's learning carrying into the next grade in Pakistan's schools (Andrabi and others 2011).

rows.label: Education: years until the participants reach working age
rows.explainer: Judgment 8 years (5-14): primary-age children in camp schools (about 10 years from work), with many secondary pupils, vocational and language students and some in higher education close to it.

rows.label: Years the earnings gain lasts
rows.explainer: GiveWell's shared figure for long-term income gains (40 years).

rows.label: Household members sharing the earnings gain
rows.explainer: GiveWell's shared figure: an earner's gain is shared in the household.

rows.label: Education: ln(consumption) gain per participant, discounted
rows.formula: ln(1 + edu_gain_sd * edu_earnings_per_sd * edu_persistence) * pv_annuity_due(1, $discount_rate, working_years) * (1 + $discount_rate) ^ (0 - edu_years_until_work) * resource_sharing_multiplier
rows.explainer: The yearly earnings gain over a working life, discounted to today from when work starts.

rows.label: Share of people in conflict-affected populations with a mental disorder
rows.explainer: The shared WHO prevalence in conflict-affected populations (@humanitarian_response.conflict_mental_disorder_prevalence, 22.1%, 18.8-25.7%); JRS's participants are displaced by conflict or persecution. Used for the light psychosocial parts of education, protection, MHPSS's community activities and pastoral work.

rows.label: Average share of an initial gain kept over its years when it fades linearly to nothing
rows.explainer: A gain that falls in a straight line from its first size to zero averages half its first size over those years.

rows.label: Education: improvement in mental health from psychosocial support in schools, for children with a disorder (SD)
rows.explainer: Judgment 0.1 SD (0-0.25): JRS integrates psychosocial support into its education programmes (p. 13); meta-analyses of school-based psychosocial programmes in humanitarian settings find small falls in post-traumatic stress and none consistent for depression (Purgato et al. 2018, Lancet Global Health), and this is a light, teacher-delivered version. As NRC's Better Learning Programme.

rows.label: Education: years the psychosocial gain lasts
rows.explainer: Judgment half a year (3-12 months), fading linearly: classroom psychosocial work runs over a term or a year and follow-ups find most of the gain gone within months. As NRC.

rows.label: Education: WELLBYs per participant from psychosocial support
Livelihoods: consumption gain per participant while it lasts
rows.explainer: Judgment 4% (1-10%): reviews of vocational training and job-search programmes in low- and middle-income countries find modest gains, employment a few percentage points and earnings a few percent (McKenzie 2017, World Bank Research Observer 32(2), https://doi.org/10.1093/wbro/lkx001); graduation programmes costing several times JRS's $203 a person (p. 17) raise consumption by 5-10% for years (Banerjee et al. 2015, Science 348(6236)). JRS's mix of training, placement and start-up support sits between, and some of it is in Europe where a job found counts the same in log terms.

rows.label: Livelihoods: years the gain lasts
rows.explainer: Judgment 3 years (1-6): a skill, job or business lasts, but displaced people move and businesses fail; graduation programmes' gains were still there three years on, training programmes' fade sooner.

rows.label: Livelihoods: ln(consumption) gain per participant, discounted
Protection and legal advice: share of participants getting legal counselling or representation
rows.explainer: Judgment 50% (30-70%): the line joins legal work for asylum seekers and refugees (status, documents, detention, family reunion), most of it in Europe, North America and Asia, with child protection, case management and detention visits; JRS publishes no split. The legal share is valued by its income gain, the rest by its mental-health gain.

rows.label: Protection and legal advice: share of legal cases resolved (status, document, release secured)
rows.explainer: Judgment 50% (30-70%): no outcome rate published; asylum cases with representation succeed more often than without, but many clients get advice only and some cases stall. As NRC's legal assistance.

rows.label: Protection and legal advice: consumption gain for a resolved case
rows.explainer: The shared figure for a resolved legal case (@humanitarian_response.legal_aid_consumption_gain, {{row:pro_consumption_gain}}, 1-15%): legal status and documents open formal work, aid registration, schooling and health care and end the risk of detention and removal.

rows.label: Protection and legal advice: years the gain lasts
rows.explainer: Judgment 3 years (1-6): a status or document lasts, but circumstances change. As NRC.

rows.label: Protection and legal advice: ln(consumption) gain per legal participant, discounted
Protection: improvement in mental health for participants with a disorder (SD)
rows.explainer: The shared figure for broad protection work (@humanitarian_response.protection_mental_health_effect_sd, 0.2 SD, 0.05-0.4): JRS's protection is child protection, case management and detention visits.

rows.label: Protection: years the gain lasts
rows.explainer: Judgment a year (6 months to 2 years), fading linearly; as NRC's and Save the Children's protection.

rows.label: Protection: WELLBYs per protection participant
MHPSS: share of participants in individual or group counselling
rows.explainer: Judgment 25% (10-40%): JRS's MHPSS joins counselling by professional and para-counsellors (the Tamil Nadu programme, p. 21) with home visits and community activities for many more; it reports moving lower-intensity work to trained refugee and volunteer community workers in 2025 (p. 20). No split published.

rows.label: MHPSS: improvement in distress from counselling, for those counselled (SD)
rows.explainer: Judgment 0.3 SD (0.15-0.5): the cluster-randomised trial of guided self-help (Self-Help Plus) for South Sudanese refugee women in Ugandan settlements found distress 0.26 SD lower at three months than with usual care (Tol et al. 2020, Lancet Global Health 8(2):e254-e263, https://doi.org/10.1016/S2214-109X(19)30504-2: 'd −0·26'); individual counselling by trained staff a little more, community workers with less supervision less.

rows.label: MHPSS: years the counselling gain lasts
rows.explainer: Judgment 9 months (3-18 months), fading linearly: trials in refugee settings measure gains at three months, and the Self-Help Plus effect had shrunk by later follow-up.

rows.label: MHPSS: people per household (stand-in)
rows.explainer: The site's household sizes for Kenya and the DRC, where much of JRS's African MHPSS works (Kakuma, the eastern DRC); the site has no figure for refugee households or most other countries.

rows.label: MHPSS: counselling's effect on the whole household, as a multiple of the client's
rows.explainer: Counselling also helps the client's household: the site's one spillover share of psychotherapy for each other member.

rows.label: MHPSS: improvement in mental health from community psychosocial activities, for participants with a disorder (SD)
rows.explainer: Judgment 0.1 SD (0-0.2): group activities, awareness and home visits without structured therapy; as the classroom psychosocial work in the education branch.

rows.label: MHPSS: years the community activities' gain lasts
rows.explainer: Judgment half a year (3-12 months), fading linearly, because group activities and home visits run for weeks or months and light psychosocial support's gains fade within months in follow-ups; low end a quarter, high end a year, as the education branch's psychosocial work.

rows.label: MHPSS: yearly suicide rate of the adults counselled, without depression's excess
rows.explainer: Judgment 10 per 100,000 a year (5-20): the WHO's global suicide rate is about 9 per 100,000 (Global Health Estimates 2019), higher among adults and among displaced people; JRS's MHPSS teams reported rising suicide attempts in 2025 (p. 20). No rate for JRS's clients' countries and ages is in the site's facts.

rows.label: MHPSS: relative risk of suicide with the distress counselled
rows.explainer: Judgment 5 (3-10): meta-analyses put the relative risk of suicide with major depression at several times the population's; clients in distress are not all depressed, so the low end is 3.

rows.label: MHPSS: share of the excess suicide risk removed while the counselling's effect lasts
rows.explainer: Judgment 15% (0-30%): a 0.3 SD fall in distress removes a modest part of the risk; no trial in these settings measures suicides.

rows.label: MHPSS: suicides averted per person counselled (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: The wellbeing family's recipe: the clients' yearly suicide rate × the excess risk with distress × the share removed, falling with the effect (half on average) over the years it lasts; the deaths come within a year or two, so no discount.

rows.label: MHPSS: value of a suicide averted (units of value)
rows.explainer: The site's value of a death at 15-49, the clients' age, times your value of a life.

rows.label: MHPSS: WELLBYs per participant
rows.formula: (mhp_focused_share * mhp_focused_effect_sd * mhp_focused_years * mhp_household_multiplier + (1 - mhp_focused_share) * share_distressed * mhp_community_effect_sd * mhp_community_years) * linear_fade_share * @wellby_factors.wellbys_per_sd_year
rows.explainer: Counselling (clients are people in distress, so no prevalence step) and the community activities (only participants with a disorder gain).

rows.label: Pastoral: improvement in mental health from spiritual accompaniment, for participants with a disorder (SD)
rows.explainer: Judgment 0.1 SD (0-0.25): reviews of spiritual and religious interventions find small falls in anxiety and depression (Gonçalves et al. 2015, Psychological Medicine 45(14):2937-2949, https://doi.org/10.1017/S0033291715001166), mostly in structured programmes; JRS's chaplaincy, including in immigration detention, is accompaniment rather than therapy. As the community psychosocial activities.

rows.label: Pastoral: years the gain lasts
rows.explainer: Judgment half a year (3-12 months), fading linearly, because accompaniment lasts as long as the visits (detention stays and camp postings of months) and no follow-up measures a lasting gain; as the community psychosocial activities.

rows.label: Pastoral: WELLBYs per participant
Reconciliation: improvement in wellbeing per participant (SD)
rows.explainer: Judgment 0.03 SD (0-0.1), for every participant: contact and dialogue programmes between groups in conflict change behaviour towards the other group (Mousa 2020, Science 369(6505):866-870, https://doi.org/10.1126/science.abb3153) more than attitudes, and no trial measures their effect on wellbeing; JRS's events and workshops are short. Violence averted is in unmodelled_benefits_adj.

rows.label: Reconciliation: years the gain lasts
rows.explainer: Judgment half a year (3-12 months), fading linearly, because the events and workshops are short and Mousa's behaviour changes were measured within months; a lasting change in relations would be the high end.

rows.label: Reconciliation: WELLBYs per participant
Health care: illness averted per person helped, in DALYs (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: Judgment 0.005 DALYs (0.001-0.02), illness only (deaths in the next row): about $18 a person before overhead buys a consultation, medicines or a referral; essential primary care in low-income countries costs a few hundred to a few thousand dollars per DALY averted (Disease Control Priorities, 3rd edition), so $20 buys 0.01-0.1 healthy years with deaths, less in Europe, where JRS helps people into national services; about half of it illness.

rows.label: Health care: deaths averted per person helped (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: Judgment 1 in 10,000 (1 in 50,000 to 1 in 2,500): the other half of the healthy years above, at about 50 healthy years per death averted (a mix of child and adult deaths); valued at the crisis deaths' age mix (value_per_death), so it moves with your value of a life.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment, emergency aid, relief and assistance
rows.explainer: Judgment 0.75 (0.5-1): the death share is a judgment without a trial, and goods valued at their cost need little evidence step; as NRC's food security.

rows.label: Share of the emergency aid, relief and assistance outcome others wouldn't have delivered
rows.explainer: Judgment 70% (45-90%): only 35% of the 2025 appeals' requirements were met (ALNAP 2026), so others rarely fill a gap a responder leaves; in Europe reception systems and other charities would have housed some. As NRC's relief lines.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment, education in emergency situations
rows.explainer: Judgment 0.6 (0.3-1): the learning gain mixes an access trial in Afghanistan and the median of other programmes' trials, the earnings link is from other settings, and displaced children move and drop out; as NRC's and Save the Children's education.

rows.label: Share of the education in emergency situations outcome others wouldn't have delivered
rows.explainer: Judgment 85% (60-100%), one question only: would another provider (the government, another of UNHCR's partners, another NGO) have run these schools and activities for the same children had JRS not been there? The children's lack of other schooling is already in edu_access_share and isn't counted again here. In 2025 cuts left teachers unpaid and schools closing (p. 13), so few others were stepping in; in some host communities others would have. As NRC's education.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment, livelihoods and economic inclusion
rows.explainer: Judgment 0.6 (0.3-0.9): the gain is a judgment from reviews of other programmes, with no evaluation of JRS's; refugees face legal limits on work that trials elsewhere don't.

rows.label: Share of the livelihoods and economic inclusion outcome others wouldn't have delivered
rows.explainer: Judgment 80% (60-100%): some participants would have found work or training anyway; programmes for refugees are scarce.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment, protection and legal advice
rows.explainer: Judgment 0.55 (0.3-0.9): no study measures what legal aid does for displaced people's consumption, and the protection effect is a judgment from more focused programmes.

rows.label: Share of the protection and legal advice outcome others wouldn't have delivered
rows.explainer: Judgment 85% (60-100%): free legal help and protection for refugees are scarce, more so after 2025's cuts; some clients would have found other legal aid. As NRC's legal assistance.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment, MHPSS
rows.explainer: Judgment 0.7 (0.4-1): counselling's effect rests on a trial in a similar population (refugees in Ugandan settlements), but delivery by less-supervised community workers and publication bias lower it; the community part is a judgment.

rows.label: Share of the MHPSS outcome others wouldn't have delivered
rows.explainer: Judgment 85% (60-100%): mental health care for refugees is scarce, and 2025's cuts closed services (p. 20); the counselling effect is already net of usual care in its trial.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment, pastoral
rows.explainer: Judgment 0.5 (0.2-0.9): reviews of spiritual interventions are of structured programmes, mostly in rich countries.

rows.label: Share of the pastoral outcome others wouldn't have delivered
rows.explainer: Judgment 90% (70-100%): few others accompany people in detention or camps spiritually.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment, reconciliation
rows.explainer: Judgment 0.4 (0.2-0.8): no trial measures wellbeing from reconciliation work.

rows.label: Share of the reconciliation outcome others wouldn't have delivered
rows.explainer: Judgment 90% (70-100%): little else of this kind in the same places.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment, health care
rows.explainer: Judgment 0.6 (0.3-1): a judgment from cost-effectiveness of primary care in general, not of JRS's services.

rows.label: Share of the health care outcome others wouldn't have delivered
rows.explainer: Judgment 60% (40-85%): UNHCR's health partners and national systems serve many of the same people; JRS fills gaps.

rows.label: JRS's share of the resources behind the outcomes (emergency aid, livelihoods, legal work, health)
rows.explainer: Judgment 85% (70-100%): JRS delivers most work itself with money that is in its accounts (UNHCR's and governments' grants included), but it leans on volunteers more than most relief agencies, in Europe especially, and on Jesuit communities' and parishes' donated space and time; those unpaid resources aren't in its cost.

rows.label: Share of credit used
rows.explainer: The charity's share of the resources behind the outcome; it applies whichever way credit is shared.

rows.label: JRS's share of the resources behind the education outcome
rows.explainer: Judgment 80% (60-100%): parents' associations raise funds for teacher salaries and school costs (p. 13, 'parents’ associations have played a vital role in raising funds to sustain teacher salaries and school running costs'), governments and UNHCR supply buildings and curricula; JRS pays most of what its schools need. As NRC's education.

rows.label: JRS's share of the resources behind the MHPSS and pastoral outcomes
rows.explainer: Judgment 80% (60-100%): JRS reports moving lower-intensity psychosocial work to 'trained refugee and volunteer community workers' (p. 20), whose unpaid time is a resource outside its accounts; chaplains are often Jesuits and other religious on stipends (their forgone pay is in salary_sacrifice, not here).

rows.label: JRS's share of the resources behind the reconciliation outcome
rows.explainer: Judgment 70% (50-100%): much of the work is with partners and volunteers (a resident-led group in East London, a podcast with two Jordanian partners, pp. 23-24).

rows.label: Delivery adjustment (participants who get the service as modelled)
rows.explainer: Judgment 85% (70-95%), every branch: the reach is JRS's own count, with donors' audits of many projects; some participants are counted in several lines or get only a light touch, and 2025's cuts interrupted services midway (Colombia served 10,000 of 30,500 planned, p. 7; MHPSS suspended in South Sudan, p. 20). Reference class: 85% for NRC's, Save the Children's and MSF's relief.

rows.label: Leverage and funging
rows.explainer: 1 (0.85-1.1): Jesuit sources (22%), multilateral (20%) and government grants (16%) are most of JRS's 2025 income (p. 33); a private gift co-funds grants and pays for what they don't cover, and kept programmes running after the US cuts (the $4m Global Appeal, p. 6). No sign it pulls in more or is displaced.

rows.label: Missing-data discount, emergency aid, relief and assistance
rows.explainer: Thin: people served is JRS's own count, but the effect is a judgment or from studies of other programmes, with no controlled evaluation or outcome data of JRS's own. So it is counted less by the shared slider, the same way in every model (docs/normalization.md 2.12).

rows.label: Benefits and harms not modelled, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: Not modelled, with signs: violence averted by reconciliation work, education's gains beyond earnings (girls' later marriage and births), livelihoods' spillovers to local markets and workers employed, and the climate-displacement research (p. 29) (+); tension with host communities over aid, dependency, and funging inside JRS (-; aid lost in conflict is in implementation_adj).
